[2] Dean: Hello. Dean.
Today, Dean is pitching Cyan Banister
[3] Cyan: Cyan.
[4] Dean: Nice to meet you.
[5] Cyan: Nice to meet you.
Charles Hudson
[6] Charles: Hey, Charles. Nice to meet you, Dean.
[7] Dean: Dean.
Elizabeth Yin
[8] Elizabeth: Elizabeth, nice to meet you.
[9] Dean: Hey Elizabeth. Dean. Nice to meet you.
Mac Conwell
[10] Mac: Mac.
[11] Dean: Mac, nice to meet you. How's it going?
and Jesse Middleton
[12] Jesse: Hey, Jesse.
[13] Dean: Hey, Jesse.
[14] Jesse: Nice to meet you, Dean.
[15] Dean: How y'all doing?
[16] Elizabeth: Great. How are you?
[17] Dean: Really good. My name's Dean. I'm the founder of ReCraft. And we have developed a new way to make beer that's 30 percent more efficient. Eight years ago, I took a month off of drinking. I just really missed that craft experience. And so I developed the most forward thinking products the beer industry has seen in decades. So that brand, Hoplark, has generated over $45 million in total revenue to date. While I was scaling Hoplark, I realized that we had created the world's most advanced hopping technology that was usable in the beer industry. So we spun off Recraft to go ignite a revolution. Hops are inherently problematic with beer. When you add them to finished beer, they absorb up to 40 percent of the liquid. And then when you remove the hops, they take a bunch of that liquid with them. With our process, none of that happens. There's zero waste at that step. So we have a bunch of consumer traction with Hoplark over the years. But we also have a partnership with Brooklyn Brewery where we're adapting all of their products to this technology and that should hit shelves later this year. So we're raising two and a half million dollars to scale this. Who wants to recraft the beer industry with me? Thank you.
[18] Elizabeth: So just to clarify, you are proposing a process, right?
[19] Dean: Yes, so we have a process, but it integrates super easy. So basically at the end of a beer brewing process, instead of dry hopping, which is like the last step, they just actually add our juice, effectively, at the end of it, and it allows it to all be way more efficient and it works just like the regular beer process.
[20] Elizabeth: But you're not making a new consumer beer brand. Is that correct?
[21] Dean: That's correct.
[22] Elizabeth: Okay.
[23] Dean: Yeah. And we've used like a similar process in Hoplark for the last six years.
[24] Elizabeth: Yeah. Yeah. Understood. Yeah.
[25] Mac: Uhh, full disclosure, at RareBreed, we have a no vice clause, so I'm not allowed to invest in anything involved with alcohol.
[26] Dean: I understand and I appreciate that.
[27] Mac: So for that, I'm out, purely just for a clause that my LPs forced me to have.
[28] Dean: No, totally understand. And I mean, I've been running a non alcoholic business for the last six years, so I get it.
[29] Mac: Would love to taste it.
[30] Dean: So on your left is a traditionally made West Coast IPA, and on your right is a West Coast IPA that's made with our technology. So we completely deconstruct the dry hopping process in a couple of different dimensions, which allow us to reconstruct it in basically whatever we want. We can make it effectively identical, or we can make it "better" depending on what the brewery is looking for. We can make it brighter. We can make it juicier. We can make it sweeter. Like there's all these subtleties that we can pull out of it.
[31] Charles: They're both really good. This one, the left one has a little more creaminess to it, like slightly, but they're both very good.
[32] Dean: Thank you So just to be clear, the product on your left is a traditionally made, dry hopped, had the 30 percent yield loss, the product on the right is with our technology.
[33] Elizabeth: I actually think I like yours better.
[34] Dean: Thank you. I mean, it's a little more balanced, maybe a little more complex, but I'm a huge flavor nerd, so I geek out on all this stuff.
[35] Jesse: So, I was curious if you can share a little bit about sort of the changes that one might have, whether it be in shelf life or anything else that changes in the output, or is it sort of all equal?
[36] Dean: Yeah. The Hoplark products have dramatically improved shelf life characteristics over beer, and we believe that hop flavors derived from our process will have dramatically improved shelf life characteristics for beer. And IPAs, if anyone's familiar with IPA sitting on a warm shelf, like, they'll get pretty nasty pretty fast. Unfortunately, it's like a challenge with the industry. We believe we can extend that pretty dramatically. So it's not just a cost savings; it could be a pretty dramatic up value.
[37] Jesse: With all of that depth in this industry, I'm curious, can you walk us through just high level, like the business itself? I mean you're buying hops, you're producing something, you're storing it, you're transporting it. Like how does all that fit together?
[38] Dean: Great question. And this is kind of the magic. So brewers are - really care about their craft and what they're able to make. And so what we do is we allow them to still utilize their own hops, their own products, their own craft. So what we're thinking about doing is bringing in the brewer's hops, processing them, and then selling a service fee for that processing. So there's no inventory. It's really just charging for the value of what we're generating and then we'll ship them the finished product.
[39] Jesse: Got it.
[40] Charles: How does it compare on a cost basis to their current methodology? if you put aside the waste piece just from a production like price comparison.
[41] Dean: Yeah so we can save up to 30 percent of the total COGS of the beer. Because we are able to extract more than what a traditional process does. We're able to save all that wasted beer. And then at the end of our process, as we've pulled all the juicy, delicious aromatics and flavor off of it, we're actually able to reuse those hops for the bittering side of the equation. Whereas a brewery would be using two different sets of hops, we only use one. So, we're able to replace 100 percent of the hops, in a brewer's system, which is dramatically more efficient for what they're trying to do.
[42] Mac: Let's say I'm starting a new craft beer today, and I want to work with you. Are you telling me I could essentially set up a brewery that's probably slightly smaller with less storage space because I don't have to hold the hops anymore?
[43] Dean: Yeah and also skip some steps at the end as well. And dry hopping takes a lot of time, whereas ours is relatively instantaneous. Which is a bigger deal than the hop storage. You can condense how much tank storage you need. Or if you're an existing brewery, you can dramatically increase your throughput because if you had a choke point on the tank side, you could run a lot more batches through.
[44] Charles: I was just going to ask you, like, given how concentrated InBev - some of these huge, I imagine they have internal R&D teams that are probably thinking about every element of the process. And how do you think about working with, like, Big Beer, for lack of a better word?
[45] Dean: Well, I think that , a) we're working on a suite of patents, We believe that we're going to get a tremendous amount of protection on it. Because of the kind of left field nature of creating these products, like we do believe we have a really big head start, and it's pretty complicated how to get to success here. So we, we believe the moat's pretty strong. We're excited to work with a lot of them.
[46] Charles: Okay.
[47] Dean: For sure.
[48] Charles: Cool.
[49] Elizabeth: What is your background prior to starting your non alcoholic beer company?
[50] Dean: So my story is, I graduated college and five months later my dad passed away super suddenly, and I got thrown into the family business, which I wasn't really planning on doing. I had a deal with my dad, we were driving down the road and when I was - I was about 21 and he turned to me and was like, do you want to run my company some day? And my answer was no, I want to do my own thing, but I got thrown into it. So I've been helping manage and guide an innovative plastic recycling company in Chicago for the last 17 years. And what happened over time is I have an amazing executive team there. I've learned how to be a chairman role and coach a team and have the team operate. I live in Boulder. It's in Chicago. They're doing awesome. Like there's been a lot of amazing business skills. My business coach tells me I'm 41 going on 61 in business years. But um, but for me, like launching Hoplark was really - in some respects, it was the start of my career because it was like the first time I was doing something that was truly me and truly something that, like, felt authentic to what I wanted to create in the world.
We’ll be right back, after the hot break.
[51] Elizabeth: So basically, if I were to summarize, after college, you ran the family business and then at some point you were able to kind of make sure to hand things off to your exec team to start Hoplark. Is that right?
[52] Dean: That's correct. Yeah.
[53] Elizabeth: I mean, in terms of discovering this process, was that you or a team member?
[54] Dean: Yeah, it was -
[55] Elizabeth: Do you have a science background?
[56] Dean: Yeah, I'm an engineer. I've come from a family of entrepreneurial engineers. We built probably like the world's coolest homebrew setup to develop the Hoplark products. So we were in the garage, it took, it probably took a hundred batches. And then I've been working over the past couple of years on essentially an amped up version of that process that'll work for this beer application.
[57] Cyan: Did you just kick off your fundraise? Or have you - do you have commitments.
[58] Dean: Yeah, we just, we just kicked it off.
[59] Cyan: Okay.
[60] Jesse: Look, I think it's super interesting. This is totally a business outside of, like, my wheelhouse. For that, like, I'm not the right fit in this, but I'm fascinated by what you're doing.
[61] Dean: Yeah. Right on. I appreciate it. Thank you.
[62] Cyan: For me, I, I'm just the wrong partner at the fund and I just, I'm outta my wheelhouse too. I don't drink beer at all, and I don't really like hops because of a previous beer incident when I was younger. I can't even smell it. But I do have a partner who did - he made Kettle & Fire and he brought in Surely, which is de-alc-ed wine. And he's really into this space. And so I would really love to run this past him.

taxonomy.label: business_model_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the startup’s revenue model, monetization approach, or service/automation mix as a driver of business viability.

taxonomy.label: business_viability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's concern that the overall business viability, model, or economics are not sufficiently compelling.

taxonomy.label: capital_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the startup will require substantial ongoing capital investment, increasing risk or misalignment with the investor’s funding capacity.

taxonomy.label: competitive_advantage_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s beliefs about what drives defensibility or sustainable competitive advantage in a market.

taxonomy.label: competitive_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the category is highly competitive, attention‐constrained, and requires heavy marketing to win, reducing the likelihood of outsized success.

taxonomy.label: competitive_landscape_inertia
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the difficulty of displacing or changing behavior of incumbents due to entrenched solutions, habits, or workflows.

taxonomy.label: deal_terms_complexity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the structure or details of deal terms (e.g., convertibles, SAFEs, preferred terms) may introduce complexity, ambiguity, or unfavorable outcomes.

taxonomy.label: decision_context_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints imposed by the specific evaluation format, environment, or context rather than the startup's fundamentals.

taxonomy.label: dilution_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the financing plan will cause excessive dilution relative to their ownership goals or stage fit.

taxonomy.label: execution_risk_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the team may not yet have demonstrated sufficient execution reliability or maturity for the risk level of the round.

taxonomy.label: founder_equity_incentive_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to ensuring founders retain sufficient ownership to remain properly motivated, aligned, and incentivized for the long-term company‐building journey.

taxonomy.label: founder_execution
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of the founders' execution ability, resourcefulness, pace, and operational grit.

taxonomy.label: founder_market_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales based on how well the founder's background, experience, or motivation aligns with the target market.

taxonomy.label: founder_qualities
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the founders' personal traits, capabilities, or appeal.

taxonomy.label: founder_skillset
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the founder's core skills or functional strengths relevant to company-building.

taxonomy.label: fund_economics_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor’s fund size, check size, or ownership goals that constrain how selective they must be when choosing investments.

taxonomy.label: fundraising_demand_signal
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the company will attract capital easily due to current or expected investor demand.

taxonomy.label: growth_projection_risk
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the company’s growth, revenue, or user‐scale projections are insufficiently modeled, unrealistic, or lack credible underlying assumptions.

taxonomy.label: investment_thesis_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's predefined investment thesis or mandate that restricts them to specific sectors, business models, or company types.

taxonomy.label: investment_upside_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's view that the risk‐reward profile offers disproportionately large potential returns relative to downside risk.

taxonomy.label: investor_domain_knowledge_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor lacking the necessary domain knowledge to effectively assess the technology, moat, competition, or overall viability of the opportunity.

taxonomy.label: investor_experience_bias
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's prior personal experiences, wins, losses, or operational history that shape their judgment of a new opportunity.

taxonomy.label: market_entry_path_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that there is a clear, reachable initial customer segment that can serve as an effective wedge into the larger market.

taxonomy.label: market_problem_validation
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor perceiving the underlying problem as real, important, or painful enough to support a venture-scale solution.

taxonomy.label: market_size_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s belief about the absolute or relative size and fluidity of the addressable market.

taxonomy.label: market_timing
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the timing is favorable or unfavorable for this market, category, or product to emerge or scale.

taxonomy.label: mission_alignment_preference
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's personal or emotional alignment with the startup's mission or purpose.

taxonomy.label: portfolio_conflict_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints arising from existing portfolio investments that create competitive conflicts preventing a new investment.

taxonomy.label: product_adoption
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to evidence that end users are adopting and using the product meaningfully.

taxonomy.label: product_appeal_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s positive perception of the product’s appeal, quality, or desirability based on their own reaction.

taxonomy.label: product_differentiation_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to how unique, defensible, or hard-to-copy the product or technology is perceived to be.

taxonomy.label: product_success_factor_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to which product components or attributes are perceived as most essential to the startup's ability to succeed.

taxonomy.label: solution_feasibility_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the proposed product or solution is technically or operationally feasible.

taxonomy.label: stage_valuation_mismatch
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of a mismatch between the company’s stage of progress and the valuation being requested.

taxonomy.label: traction_repeatability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that current traction, usage, or revenue signals are too early or insufficiently repeatable to support scaling.

taxonomy.label: unit_economics_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the business benefits from structurally attractive unit economics, such as profitable or self-reinforcing customer acquisition.

taxonomy.label: venture_scale_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the companys market dynamics, ceiling, or competitive landscape limit its ability to achieve venture-scale outcomes.

taxonomy.label: investor_value_add_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the investor can contribute meaningful help, networks, or domain value beyond capital to this specific company.

taxonomy.label: founder_coachability_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how receptive the founder is to feedback, advice, or course-correction and their ability to read and respond to the room.

taxonomy.label: founder_communication_quality
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the founder's clarity, articulation, command of their numbers, and storytelling ability when presenting the business.

taxonomy.label: founder_motivation_authenticity
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the genuineness, personal connection, or origin of the founder's drive to work on this particular problem.

taxonomy.label: go_to_market_strategy_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how the company will reach and acquire customers, including sales motion, channel scalability, and cost of acquisition.

taxonomy.label: founder_investor_vision_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the founder's intended direction or focus for the company aligns with the path the investor believes in or would back.

taxonomy.label: corporate_structure_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the company's legal entity, incorporation, jurisdiction, or IP-ownership structure as a barrier or condition to investing.
